scenes.tts: Sanger spent twelve years on a single molecule. He worked on Tennis Court Road in Cambridge, a Quaker conscientious objector who had spent the war scrubbing hospital toilets with a mop, and he called himself "academically not brilliant" — he had taken three years over the first part of his degree.

scenes.tts: Insulin fought him: its disulfide bonds rearranged themselves mid-experiment, the molecule effectively lying to him about its own structure, until he caught them with a trace of thioglycolic acid.

scenes.tts: In 1955 he published the answer — fifty-one amino acids, two chains, three sulfur bridges, in one fixed order.

scenes.tts: He did it again with DNA in 1977, sequenced the first complete DNA genome, and took a second Nobel in 1980, the only person of the century to win the chemistry prize twice. He declined a knighthood because he did not want to be different, and retired at sixty-five to his garden.

scenes.tts: When the great genome center at Hinxton asked to take his name, his only condition was a sentence that could stand as his whole creed: it had better be good.
